stem: You're deciding which of today's Claude Code tasks to hand to subagents to keep your main context lean. Which tasks does the subagents guide say fit a subagent better than the main conversation?

choices.text: Iterating on a UI layout with you, adjusting it after each round of feedback
choices.reason: Frequent back-and-forth or iterative refinement belongs in the main conversation.

choices.text: Running the full test suite and reporting which tests failed
choices.reason: Correct: a task whose verbose output you don’t need in the main context fits a subagent; only the summary returns.

choices.text: A quick one-line fix to a typo in a config file
choices.reason: Quick, targeted changes stay in the main conversation; a subagent that isn’t a fork starts fresh and may need time to gather context.

choices.text: Auditing log files with tools restricted to reading, so no file can be edited
choices.reason: Correct: subagents fit work that needs specific tool restrictions or permissions and that is self-contained enough to return a summary.

choices.text: Planning, implementing and testing one feature whose phases share a lot of context
choices.reason: Phases that share significant context, such as planning, implementation and testing, stay in the main conversation.

takeaway: Hand off verbose, self-contained or permission-scoped work; keep iterative, shared-context and quick tasks in the main conversation.
explanation: A handoff pays off when the subagent's work would otherwise flood your context and only a summary needs to come back, or when the work needs its own tool restrictions. The test run and the read-only log audit both qualify. Choice e is the tempting one, since a big feature sounds like a lot of tokens, but its phases depend on shared context that a fresh subagent wouldn't have.

stem: Your team wants every compaction in a project's Claude Code sessions to keep test output and code changes, without anyone having to remember to type `/compact` with focus instructions. What does the costs guide suggest?

choices.text: Turn off auto-compaction, so that nothing is ever summarized away
choices.reason: Auto-compaction is how Claude Code summarizes history as it approaches context limits; turning it off doesn’t tell a summary what to keep.

choices.text: Add a "Compact instructions" section to the project’s CLAUDE.md saying what to focus on
choices.reason: The guide shows customizing compaction in the root CLAUDE.md, for example "focus on test output and code changes".

choices.text: Have everyone run `/clear` instead, which keeps test output by default
choices.reason: `/clear` starts fresh rather than summarizing, so it keeps nothing from the session.

choices.text: Move test output into a skill, so compaction can’t summarize it away
choices.reason: Skills load on demand to keep base context small; they don’t control what a compaction summary keeps.

takeaway: Put standing compaction guidance in CLAUDE.md; use `/compact <focus>` for one-off steering.
explanation: Compaction keeps context small but can drop what matters, so Claude Code lets you tell it what to preserve. The stem asks for a standing rule, not a per-command one, and the costs guide shows exactly that: a compact-instructions section in the project's CLAUDE.md. Choice d sounds clever, but skills change when content loads, not what a summary keeps.

stem: Your Claude Code subagents run simple log-summarizing tasks, but they inherit your session's Opus model and their usage keeps climbing. What does the costs guide suggest?

choices.text: Move the log work back into the main conversation, where it adds no extra cost
choices.reason: Verbose log output would then fill the main context; the guide recommends delegating log processing to subagents.

choices.text: Raise the effort level so the subagents finish their work in fewer turns
choices.reason: For simpler tasks, the guide reduces cost by lowering the effort level, not raising it.

choices.text: Set `model: haiku` in those subagents’ configuration
choices.reason: For simple subagent tasks the guide says to specify `model: haiku`, because a subagent’s own requests still draw on your usage.

choices.text: Leave it, because subagent requests don’t draw on your usage at all
choices.reason: The guide says a subagent’s own requests still draw on your usage.

takeaway: Subagents spend tokens of their own; give simple ones a smaller model such as Haiku.
explanation: A subagent keeps verbose work out of your main context, but its own requests are still billed, at the price of whichever model it runs on. Simple summarizing doesn't need Opus, so the guide's fix is a cheaper model in the subagent's configuration. Choice a is tempting because it removes the subagent, but it pours the verbose logs back into the main conversation.

stem: Your Python service defines its extraction result as a Pydantic model, hand-maintains a matching JSON schema for `output_config.format`, and parses the reply text itself. The model and the schema keep drifting apart. What does the structured-outputs guide recommend?

choices.text: Paste the Pydantic class into the system prompt and ask for matching JSON
choices.reason: Prompting alone gives no guarantee; structured outputs enforce the schema through constrained decoding.

choices.text: Drop the schema and retry in code whenever a reply fails validation
choices.reason: Structured outputs make retries for schema violations unnecessary; dropping the schema throws that guarantee away.

choices.text: Pass the Pydantic model to `client.messages.parse()` and read `parsed_output`
choices.reason: Correct: the SDK transforms the model’s schema, sends it as `output_config.format`, validates the response and returns the parsed model.

choices.text: Turn the model into a strict tool and read the reply from its `tool_use` input
choices.reason: Strict tool use validates how Claude calls your functions; JSON outputs control the response format, which is what you need here.

takeaway: Let the SDK own the schema: `client.messages.parse()` with a **Pydantic** (or Zod) model sends the schema, validates the reply and returns a typed result.
explanation: When code types and the schema are kept by hand in two places, they drift. The guide's recommended Python path is to pass the Pydantic model to `client.messages.parse()`, which sends the schema, validates the reply and returns `parsed_output` (C), so the model is the single source of truth. Option D is tempting because strict tools also enforce schemas, but they shape tool calls, not the response format. A and B give up the schema guarantee.

stem: Claude drafts press releases from your product briefs. Legal requires every claim to be traceable to a brief, with unsupported claims removed before review. Which technique from Anthropic's hallucination guide fits best?

choices.text: Best-of-N: run the prompt several times and compare the drafts for inconsistent claims
choices.reason: Inconsistencies across outputs could indicate hallucinations, but comparing drafts doesn't tie each claim to a source.

choices.text: Have Claude find a supporting quote for each drafted claim and retract any it can't support
choices.reason: Correct: verifying with citations makes the response auditable; if Claude can't find a supporting quote for a claim, it must retract it.

choices.text: Chain-of-thought verification: review Claude's summarized reasoning before accepting the final draft
choices.reason: Reviewing Claude's summarized reasoning can reveal faulty logic or assumptions, but it doesn't check each claim against the briefs.

choices.text: Give Claude explicit permission to say "I don't know" when the briefs lack information
choices.reason: That helps when information is missing, but it doesn't check each drafted claim against the briefs or remove unsupported ones.

takeaway: For auditable output, have Claude back **each claim with a quote** and retract what it can't support; still validate critical facts.
explanation: The constraint to notice is that every claim must be **traceable to a brief**, with unsupported claims removed. Verifying with citations does exactly that: Claude finds a supporting quote for each claim and retracts any it can't support, making the output auditable (Option B). Best-of-N (A) is the tempting trap because it does help detect hallucinations, but comparing drafts never ties a claim to a source. C reviews reasoning rather than claims, and D only helps when information is missing.

stem: Your language-tutor app gives Claude a persona with a one-line role in the system prompt. It stays in character in normal chats but breaks character when learners ask unusual questions. What does Anthropic's consistency guide suggest?

choices.text: Prefill each assistant turn with the character's name and a short reminder of the persona
choices.reason: The guide's advice for staying in character is a detailed role and prepared scenarios; prefilling also isn't supported on Claude 4.6 and later models.

choices.text: Switch to structured outputs with a strict JSON schema describing the persona's fields
choices.reason: Structured outputs guarantee JSON schema conformance; they don't define a personality or prepare it for unusual situations.

choices.text: Break every reply into a chain of smaller prompts, each with its own copy of the one-line role
choices.reason: The guide suggests chaining for complex tasks; for role-based apps it points to the system prompt role and prepared scenarios.

choices.text: Detail the persona's background and traits, and list common scenarios with expected replies
choices.reason: Correct: detail helps Claude emulate and generalize the character's traits, and prepared scenarios help it handle diverse situations without breaking character.

takeaway: Keep a persona steady with a **detailed role** in the system prompt plus **prepared scenarios** and expected responses.
explanation: Anthropic's consistency guide says a persona stays steady when the system prompt gives a **detailed role** and **prepared scenarios** with expected replies. The clue here is the one-line role failing on unusual questions: more detail helps Claude generalize the character's traits, and prepared scenarios cover diverse situations, which is Option D. A is tempting but prefilling isn't supported on Claude 4.6 and later models. B only enforces JSON shape, and C points to chaining, which the guide suggests for complex tasks rather than for role-based apps.

stem: An agent works on a task that runs for hours. Each time its context is reset, it loses track of what it has already finished and repeats work. Which technique from Anthropic's context engineering post addresses this?

choices.text: Load the full transcript of every earlier session into the system prompt
choices.reason: The post treats context as finite and warns of context pollution; it aims for the smallest set of high-signal tokens, not every past transcript.

choices.text: Have it write progress notes to a file outside the context and read them back later
choices.reason: Correct: in structured note-taking the agent persists notes outside the context window, such as a NOTES.md file, and pulls them back in later.

choices.text: Restart the task from the beginning after every reset so nothing is skipped
choices.reason: The post's example agent reads its own notes after context resets and **continues** its multi-hour work rather than starting over.

choices.text: Shorten each of the agent's replies so that more turns fit before the reset
choices.reason: Shorter replies still leave nothing that survives a reset; the post's technique keeps notes outside the context window.

takeaway: Long tasks outlive one context window: have the agent keep **notes outside the context** and read them back after a reset.
explanation: The problem is lost state across context resets, so the fix has to live outside the context window. Structured note-taking does that: the agent writes progress notes (like a NOTES.md file) and reads them back to continue (B). Option A is the tempting one, but piling every old transcript into the prompt bloats the context the post says to keep small and high-signal.

source.title: Effective context engineering for AI agents

stem: Early in a long Claude Code session you told Claude, in chat, never to edit the generated API client. After `/compact`, Claude starts editing it again. What does Claude Code's memory guide suggest so the rule persists?

choices.text: Add the rule to the project-root CLAUDE.md, which is re-read after compaction
choices.reason: Correct: project-root CLAUDE.md survives compaction, because Claude re-reads it from disk and re-injects it; chat-only instructions can be lost.

choices.text: Repeat the rule in chat after each compaction so the next summary keeps it
choices.reason: The guide's fix for conversation-only instructions is to add them to CLAUDE.md so they persist, not to keep retyping them.

choices.text: Keep the rule in chat, since every instruction survives compaction unchanged
choices.reason: The guide says an instruction that disappears after compaction was often given only in conversation.

choices.text: Move the rule into a CLAUDE.md in a subdirectory that Claude rarely opens
choices.reason: The guide lists a nested CLAUDE.md that hasn't reloaded yet as one reason an instruction can vanish after compaction.

takeaway: Rules given only in chat can be lost to compaction; put lasting rules in the project's **CLAUDE.md**, which is re-read afterwards.
explanation: Compaction summarizes the conversation, so an instruction that lived only in chat can drop out. The project-root CLAUDE.md is re-read from disk and re-injected after `/compact`, which keeps the rule in place (A). Option D is the tempting one because it also uses CLAUDE.md, but a nested file loads again only on demand, so it may not be back yet.

stem: One API call asks Claude to draft a policy summary, critique the draft against a checklist and then revise it. When the result is poor, the team can't tell which stage went wrong. What does Anthropic's prompting guide suggest?

choices.text: Spell out every stage in more detail inside the same single prompt
choices.reason: The guide says explicit chaining is useful when you need to **inspect intermediate outputs**, which one combined call doesn't expose.

choices.text: Ask Claude to score its own final answer at the end of the same reply
choices.reason: A final score still hides the draft and the review; the guide's pattern makes each step a separate call.

choices.text: Run the three stages in parallel calls and keep whichever output is best
choices.reason: The stages depend on each other: the guide's self-correction chain feeds the draft into the review, then the review into the refinement.

choices.text: Chain it: draft, review and refine as separate calls you can log and check
choices.reason: Correct: in the guide's self-correction chain each step is a separate API call, so you can log, evaluate or branch at any point.

takeaway: Need to see where a multistep task fails? **Chain** the steps as separate API calls you can log and evaluate.
explanation: The deciding detail is that the team can't see the intermediate outputs. Prompt chaining splits the work into separate calls (draft, review, refine), so each stage's output can be logged, evaluated or branched on (D). Option A is the tempting one, but a more detailed single prompt still returns only the final result.

stem: Your public app inserts each user's free-text request into a prompt template. Some users paste well-known jailbreak phrasing to override your instructions. Which input-handling step does Anthropic's guide suggest before the text reaches Claude?

choices.text: Insert the request unchanged and rely on Claude's resilience alone
choices.reason: The guide says Claude is inherently resilient, yet still recommends added steps such as input validation to strengthen guardrails.

choices.text: Filter input for known injection patterns, such as with an LLM screen
choices.reason: Correct: the guide suggests filtering user input for known injection patterns, and an LLM given known jailbreak language as examples can screen it.

choices.text: Ask users in the app's help text not to paste instructions into requests
choices.reason: A request to users doesn't check anything; the guide's step filters the input itself before it reaches Claude.

choices.text: Move the user's text into the system prompt so it carries your authority
choices.reason: The guide keeps untrusted content out of system prompts; putting user text there gives it more weight, not less.

takeaway: Sanitize before Claude sees it: **filter user input** for known injection patterns, for example with an LLM validation screen.
explanation: Input sanitization means checking untrusted text before it enters your prompt. The guide's step is input validation: filter for known injection patterns, optionally with an LLM screen primed with known jailbreak language (B). Option A is the tempting one, since Claude is resilient to such attacks, but the guide adds validation on top of that resilience rather than relying on it.

stem: Your agent runs every user message through an injection filter, but passes the web pages its fetch tool returns straight to Claude. What does Anthropic's guide suggest for that tool content?

choices.text: Validate or screen tool results too, before they reach Claude
choices.reason: Correct: the guide says to apply the input-validation patterns to tool results as well, and to screen tool outputs before Claude acts on them.

choices.text: Leave them unscreened, since only users attempt prompt injection
choices.reason: The guide describes **indirect** injection, where third-party content such as a fetched page carries the instructions.

choices.text: Copy the page text into the system prompt so it's weighed like your rules
choices.reason: The guide says to deliver third-party content only in tool results, never in system prompts.

choices.text: Add your own note inside each tool result telling Claude to ignore injections
choices.reason: The guide says not to put your instructions in tool results: Claude may ignore them or flag them as a possible injection.

takeaway: Sanitize every input channel: run **tool results** through the same validation or screening as user input.
explanation: Untrusted text can arrive through tools as well as from users, so input checks belong on both. The guide says the same validation patterns can be applied to tool results, with a lightweight screen before Claude acts on them (A). Option D is the tempting one, but instructions placed inside a tool result may be ignored or flagged as an injection.

stem: Your service extracts line items from long invoices with a JSON schema and writes each reply straight to the database. On one very long invoice the reply has `stop_reason: "max_tokens"`, and its JSON ends partway through the items array. What should the code do?

choices.text: Close the open brackets so the JSON parses, then save the items that came through
choices.reason: A cut-off reply may be incomplete and not match the schema. Patching the brackets saves a partial record that looks complete to everything downstream.

choices.text: Treat the reply as incomplete, don't save it, and retry with a higher `max_tokens`
choices.reason: Correct: the guide says a `max_tokens` cut-off may be incomplete and not match your schema, and to retry with a higher `max_tokens` to get the complete structured output.

choices.text: Save it as is, since the schema guarantees that every reply is valid and parseable
choices.reason: The guarantee holds in most cases, not all: the guide lists a `max_tokens` cut-off as one case where the output may not match your schema.

choices.text: Retry the identical request with backoff, since the cut-off was a transient API error
choices.reason: The response came back normally, with `stop_reason: "max_tokens"`; it isn't an API error. The guide's fix is a higher `max_tokens`, not an unchanged retry.

takeaway: Check `stop_reason` before trusting structured output: a `max_tokens` cut-off is incomplete, so retry with more room instead of saving it.
explanation: Structured outputs guarantee schema compliance in most cases, but a reply cut off at `max_tokens` may be incomplete and miss the schema. The detail that decides it is the stop reason in the stem: the reply ended because it ran out of room, so the fix is more room, not repair. Choice a is tempting because it rescues some data, but it writes a partial record that downstream code will treat as the whole invoice.

diagram.caption: A cut-off reply never reaches the database.

stem: Claude turns refund requests into JSON that matches your schema every time, and your code sends each refund straight to the payments API. In testing, one well-formed reply asks to refund more than the order's total. Where should a value like this be caught?

choices.text: Nowhere new: a reply that matches the schema has been checked already, so it's safe
choices.reason: Matching a schema doesn't make a value right or safe. OWASP's guidance is zero trust: treat the model like any other user and validate its responses.

choices.text: Only in the payments system, after the request is sent, since your code just passes it on
choices.reason: OWASP says to validate model responses before they reach backend functions. Leaving it to the payments system lets the bad refund leave your service first.

choices.text: In your code, by checking rules such as amount against order total before the API call
choices.reason: Correct: treat the model like any other user and apply validation to its responses before they reach backend functions such as the payments API.

choices.text: In the prompt, by telling Claude never to ask for more than the order total
choices.reason: An instruction isn't validation. OWASP's mitigation is to validate the model's responses in code before they are used by backend functions.

takeaway: Treat model output like untrusted user input: check its values against your rules before it reaches a backend.
explanation: OWASP lists improper output handling as a top risk for LLM apps: model output passed to backend functions without enough validation. The reply in the stem is well-formed but wrong, so only a check on the values, made before the payments call, stops it. Choice a is tempting because the reply passed the schema, but a correct shape is not a correct amount.

stem: Your sales-lead schema marks `phone` as a required string. Many emails include no phone number, and in those replies Claude fills in a plausible-looking one. Sales is now calling numbers nobody gave you. Which change best addresses this at the source?

choices.text: Let `phone` be null, and tell Claude to use null when an email gives no number
choices.reason: Correct: explicitly giving Claude permission to admit it doesn't know can drastically reduce false information. A null value is that way out for a field the email lacks.

choices.text: Add a stricter phone format to the schema so that invented numbers fail to match
choices.reason: An invented number can be perfectly well-formed. A format check tests the shape of the value, not whether the email ever contained it.

choices.text: Raise `max_tokens` so Claude has room to search each email more carefully
choices.reason: Output length isn't the problem: these emails have no number to find. What's missing is a sanctioned way for Claude to say so.

choices.text: Keep `phone` required, and retry each reply until its number looks like a real one
choices.reason: Retrying can't produce a number the email doesn't contain. It only gives Claude more chances to invent one that looks convincing.

takeaway: If a field can be missing from the source, give Claude a legitimate way to say so, such as null, instead of forcing a value.
explanation: A required string must be filled on every reply, so when the email has no number, Claude has nothing true to put there. Anthropic's hallucination guide says explicitly allowing Claude to admit uncertainty can drastically reduce false information, and a nullable field is how a schema allows it. It reduces rather than eliminates the problem, so still validate critical fields. Choice b is tempting, but a made-up number can be perfectly well-formed, so a format check lets it through.

stem: You're writing the handler for a ticket-routing request whose JSON schema has a `priority` enum of `low`, `medium` and `high`. Downstream, a router switches on `priority` to pick a queue. Which two rules should the handler follow?

choices.text: Treat any reply with HTTP 200 as schema-valid and pass it on to the router
choices.reason: A refusal also returns a 200 status code, with `stop_reason: "refusal"`, and its output may not match your schema.

choices.text: Check `stop_reason` first, and handle a refusal apart from normal replies
choices.reason: Correct: when Claude refuses, the response has `stop_reason: "refusal"` and the refusal takes precedence over the schema, so it can't be routed like a normal reply.

choices.text: If `priority` fails to parse, set it to `low` and send the ticket on
choices.reason: A silent default hides the failure: an urgent ticket whose reply failed would quietly land in the low-priority queue.

choices.text: Compare `priority` with the enum values case-insensitively before routing
choices.reason: Correct: structured outputs don't guarantee the capitalization of string `enum` values, and the guide says to compare them case-insensitively.

choices.text: Drop the schema checks, since constrained decoding means violations can't occur
choices.reason: Compliance holds in most cases, not all: the guide lists refusals and `max_tokens` cut-offs as cases where output may not match the schema.

takeaway: Before passing structured output on, check `stop_reason` and normalize enum casing; a 200 status alone doesn't mean the reply fits.
explanation: Structured outputs guarantee schema compliance in most cases, but your handler still meets the exceptions: a refusal arrives as a normal 200 response, and enum capitalization isn't guaranteed. The router in the stem switches on `priority`, so either one would misroute tickets if left unhandled. Choice c is tempting because it keeps tickets moving, but it silently sends failed replies to the wrong queue.

stem: Your team wants to add a JSON output schema (`output_config.format`) to every Claude feature you run. For which two features is a JSON output schema the wrong tool?

choices.text: A help-desk chat whose replies stream to customers as prose and are never parsed
choices.reason: Correct: structured outputs exist to give code valid, parseable output for downstream processing. A reply that only people read has nothing downstream to parse.

choices.text: Pulling the vendor, date and total out of each invoice into a database
choices.reason: Extracting structured data from unstructured text is one of the guide's common use cases for structured outputs.

choices.text: Sorting each incoming support ticket into one of a fixed set of categories
choices.reason: Classifying content into structured categories is one of the guide's common use cases.

choices.text: An agent that decides mid-task to open a ticket in your tracker, then carries on
choices.reason: Correct: acting on a system mid-task is a tool call. JSON outputs control what Claude says; strict tool use validates how Claude calls your functions.

choices.text: Building the response body that another service's API expects to receive
choices.reason: Generating API-ready responses is one of the guide's common use cases for structured outputs.

takeaway: Use JSON outputs when code parses Claude's answer; plain text suits replies people read, and tools suit actions.
explanation: JSON outputs shape what Claude says so downstream code can parse it. What decides each case is who consumes the output: the chat reply is read by people, and the agent needs to act mid-task, which a tool call does (with strict tool use when its inputs must be valid). The other three are the guide's own use cases: data extraction, classification and API response formatting.

stem: Your research assistant answers from documents you retrieve and returns JSON with an answer plus a `source_ids` list. Every reply matches the schema, but audits find some IDs point to no document you supplied. Which approach best keeps unsupported claims from reaching users?

choices.text: Give the schema a stricter ID format, so every source ID has to look like a real one
choices.reason: A made-up ID can look exactly like a real one. A format check can't tell you whether a supplied document actually supports the claim.

choices.text: Trust the replies, since an ID that matches the schema must refer to a real document
choices.reason: The schema fixes the format only. The guide notes that even advanced models can produce text inconsistent with the context they were given.

choices.text: Remove `source_ids` from the schema, so Claude has no way to cite something wrong
choices.reason: Dropping citations makes answers harder to audit. The guide recommends having Claude cite sources for each claim, not removing them.

choices.text: Restrict Claude to your documents, require a supporting quote per claim, check IDs
choices.reason: Correct: the guide recommends restricting Claude to provided documents, backing each claim with a quote and retracting claims without one, and validating critical information.

takeaway: A well-formed citation can still be unsupported: ground Claude in the supplied documents and verify each reference.
explanation: A schema fixes a reply's shape, not whether its references exist. The guide's grounding techniques target exactly this: restrict Claude to the supplied documents, make each claim cite a supporting quote, retract claims that lack one, and still validate critical information yourself. Choice a is tempting, but an invented ID can be perfectly well-formed, so a format check lets it through.

stem: Claude reads sales emails and returns schema-valid JSON with a `company` string. Your code builds a SQL lookup by pasting `company` into the query text. A tester sends an email whose company name is written to end the query and add a command of its own. What protects the database?

choices.text: Pass `company` to the query as a bound parameter, not pasted into the SQL text
choices.reason: Correct: OWASP says to use parameterized queries or prepared statements for all database operations involving LLM output, and to treat the model like any other user.

choices.text: Nothing extra, since a field that matches the schema can only hold a safe string
choices.reason: A string field can hold any text, SQL included. OWASP lists LLM-generated SQL run without proper parameterization as a path to SQL injection.

choices.text: Tell Claude in the system prompt to remove any SQL from the fields it returns
choices.reason: OWASP notes that LLM output can be controlled by prompt input, as this email shows. Its fix sits in your code: parameterized queries for database work with LLM output.

choices.text: Log each reply that contains SQL keywords, so the team can review it afterwards
choices.reason: OWASP recommends monitoring LLM output for unusual patterns, but alongside parameterized queries, not instead. By the time anyone reads the log, the query has run.

takeaway: Schema-valid strings are still untrusted input: bind them as query parameters, never paste them into SQL.
explanation: OWASP's improper output handling risk is model output passed downstream without enough validation, and LLM-generated SQL run without parameterization is one of its named examples. A schema fixes the reply's shape, not what a string field says, so the email's crafted text reaches the query intact. Choice c is tempting because it states the rule, but output the input can steer can't be trusted to follow it. A bound parameter keeps the text as data whatever it says.

stem: This job turns transcribed business cards into sales leads. A few runs crash on the last line with `KeyError: 'email'`, even though `json.loads` succeeds. What is the cause, and the fix?

choices.text: The reply hit `max_tokens` partway through, so the JSON lost its last field
choices.reason: The code already raises on `max_tokens` and `refusal`, and `json.loads` succeeded, so this reply is complete JSON.

choices.text: Structured outputs reorder properties, so `email` comes back under another key
choices.reason: The docs' ordering rule moves required properties ahead of optional ones. It changes where a property appears, not its name.

choices.text: The API ignores `required` in a raw schema, so the reply skipped the schema
choices.reason: `required` is on the list of supported schema features, and a raw schema in `output_config.format` is a documented way to send it.

choices.text: `email` isn't in `required`, so a valid reply can leave it out; handle the missing key
choices.reason: Correct: properties not listed in `required` are optional. A card with no email gives schema-valid JSON without that key, so read it with `.get()` and handle `None`.

takeaway: A schema-valid reply can leave out any property not in `required`, so code must handle optional keys being absent.
explanation: Structured outputs make the reply match the schema, and this schema lists only `name` and `company` as required, so `email` is optional. A card without an email produces valid JSON with no `email` key, and `lead["email"]` raises. Choice a is tempting because truncation is the usual way a structured reply breaks, but the code already rejects `max_tokens` stops and the JSON parsed.

stem: This extractor works on short invoices. On a very long one, `json.loads` raises even though the request uses a JSON schema. What is the most likely cause, and the fix?

choices.text: The schema was ignored, because JSON outputs only work through `client.messages.parse()`
choices.reason: `parse()` is the recommended helper, but sending a raw schema in `output_config.format` on `create` is documented too.

choices.text: The reply hit `max_tokens`; check for it and retry with a higher limit
choices.reason: Correct: at `stop_reason: "max_tokens"` the output may be incomplete and miss the schema. The docs say to retry with a higher `max_tokens`.

choices.text: Long inputs make Claude write prose before the JSON; strip everything before the first `{`
choices.reason: With JSON outputs, the text block holds JSON matching your schema. The documented cause of incomplete JSON is the token limit.

choices.text: The API had a transient fault; retry the identical request with exponential backoff
choices.reason: A `max_tokens` stop isn't an API fault: the reply ran out of room. The same request with the same 512-token limit would stop again.

takeaway: Schema guarantees hold for complete replies only; check `stop_reason` for `max_tokens` as well as `refusal` before parsing.
explanation: The handler checks for a refusal, one documented way a structured reply can miss its schema, but not another: hitting `max_tokens`. A long invoice produces a long JSON array, and 512 tokens isn't enough, so the text ends partway through. Choice d is tempting because the failure is intermittent, but it tracks input length, not chance, and retrying unchanged repeats it.

stem: Structured outputs don't support numeric bounds such as `maximum`, so your team wrote the refund cap into the field's description. A reply with `amount_cents: 9000` reached `issue_refund`. What should change?

choices.text: Check `amount_cents` against the cap in code before calling `issue_refund`
choices.reason: Correct: the API constrains the reply to the supported schema, where `amount_cents` only has to be an integer. The docs leave unsupported constraints to validation in your code.

choices.text: Nothing: a reply that matches the schema also follows every field description
choices.reason: A description is text for Claude to read, not a constraint. The schema only requires an integer, and 9000 is one.

choices.text: Raise `max_tokens`, so Claude has room to apply the cap from the description
choices.reason: The code already rejects `max_tokens` stops, so this reply was complete. The limit on output length doesn't decide which number Claude writes.

choices.text: Move the refund into a tool marked `"strict": true`, so its inputs obey the cap
choices.reason: Strict tool use makes inputs follow the `input_schema`, and it shares JSON outputs' schema limits, numeric constraints included. A description is still only guidance.

takeaway: A schema-shaped reply can still carry a wrong value; check business limits in code before acting on it.
explanation: The reply is complete, valid JSON that matches the schema, because `amount_cents` only has to be an integer. The cap lives in a description, which Claude reads but the API doesn't enforce, so the one rule that mattered was never checked. It has to be checked in code, between parsing and the side effect. Choice b is the tempting belief that "matches the schema" means "follows every instruction in it".

stem: A short, well-specified prompt labels incoming emails as `billing`, `bug` or `other`, and it passes your eval with instructions alone. A teammate wants to add a handful of labelled examples "to be safe". What does that most likely do?

choices.text: Adds prompt text to every request for little or no gain, since nothing in the output needs steering
choices.reason: Correct: the page recommends examples to "steer Claude's output format, tone, and structure" and improve consistency. A prompt that already passes has no such failure, so the examples are extra prompt text with no job.

choices.text: Raises accuracy noticeably, because shown examples always beat written instructions, even on a task that passes
choices.reason: Examples are "one of the most reliable ways to steer" format and structure; the page doesn't claim they beat clear instructions on every task, and there is no failure here for them to correct.

choices.text: Swaps in a fine-tuned variant that has learned the shown pattern, so the labels now come from a different model
choices.reason: Examples are prompt content, wrapped in `<example>` tags so Claude can tell them from instructions; they don't change the model that runs.

choices.text: Makes the labels deterministic, so the same email receives the same label on every run from now on
choices.reason: Examples "improve accuracy and consistency"; nothing on the page says they make outputs deterministic.

takeaway: Add examples to fix a format or consistency failure you've observed, not as insurance on a prompt that already passes.
explanation: Examples are a targeted tool: the docs recommend them when format, tone, structure or consistency need steering. The deciding detail is that this prompt already passes its eval with instructions alone, so there is no failure for examples to address, and every request would carry the extra text. Option b is the trap: examples are reliable for the failures they fix, not a universal accuracy upgrade.

stem: Your clause-extraction prompt describes the output layout in words, yet Claude keeps arranging the fields differently. You add a handful of real input-to-output examples in `<example>` tags. Which prediction is accurate?

choices.text: The examples permanently retrain the model on your layout, so later requests can leave them out
choices.reason: Examples are prompt content; nothing is trained or stored between requests. Drop them and the steering goes with them.

choices.text: The layout becomes much more consistent: examples are among the most reliable ways to steer format and structure
choices.reason: Correct: "Examples are one of the most reliable ways to steer Claude's output format, tone, and structure." Keep them relevant and diverse, and include 3–5 for best results.

choices.text: Nothing changes: output structure is controlled only by `effort` and the choice of model, never by prompt content such as examples
choices.reason: The page names examples as the reliable lever for format and structure; they are prompt content that works on any current model.

choices.text: Each request gets cheaper, because showing the pattern lets Claude answer with fewer tokens
choices.reason: Examples add text to the prompt. The page recommends them for format, tone, structure and consistency, not as a cost lever.

takeaway: When structure is invented or drifts, show it: a few relevant, diverse examples beat more adjectives.
explanation: The failure type decides the technique: the instructions describe the layout but the structure still varies, which is exactly what examples fix. The docs call few-shot examples one of the most reliable ways to steer format and structure, recommending 3–5 relevant, diverse ones in `<example>` tags. Option a is the trap: examples live in the prompt and must stay there; nothing is retrained.

stem: The first four calls were correct. From T6 the agent picks the wrong tool, then gives up without the clause-rule tool ever running. Nothing was rejected or truncated. Identify the mechanism and the targeted fix.

snippet.code:
SESSION TRACE  (lease-review agent, 1M window)
T1 user: "Can tenant T-88 end the lease early?
         Apply the clause rules and answer."
T2 asst: tool_use fetch_lease_section(sec=1)
T2 user: tool_result  41,200 tokens
T3 asst: tool_use fetch_lease_section(sec=2)
T3 user: tool_result  39,800 tokens
T4 asst: tool_use fetch_lease_section(sec=3)
T4 user: tool_result  44,100 tokens
T5 asst: tool_use fetch_lease_section(sec=4)
T5 user: tool_result  40,600 tokens
T6 asst: tool_use search_precedents("early exit")
T6 user: tool_result  33,000 tokens
T7 asst: tool_use search_precedents("tenant T-88")
T7 user: tool_result  31,500 tokens
T8 asst: text "I could not determine whether

note: apply_exit_clause_rule never called;

choices.text: The `search_precedents` description is too vague; add a sentence saying when not to use it, and Claude will pick `apply_exit_clause_rule`
choices.reason: Selection was right for four turns with the same descriptions. The drift began only after some 165k tokens of raw results had piled up, which points at context, not at the schema.

choices.text: Accumulated raw results are degrading recall of the instructions; clear each result once used and compact before continuing
choices.reason: Correct: "As token count grows, accuracy and recall degrade, a phenomenon known as context rot." Tool results count toward the window; the page offers tool result clearing and compaction for exactly this.

choices.text: Raise `max_tokens` so Claude has room to finish its reasoning in T8 and finally reach the rule tool
choices.reason: Nothing stopped on `max_tokens`. That cap limits output length; the problem here is on the input side, where the request keeps growing.

choices.text: Switch to a model with a larger context window so all four lease sections fit with room to spare
choices.reason: The 1M window was never exceeded. "More context isn't automatically better": the degradation comes from how much is in context, not from running out of room.

takeaway: Tool outputs spend the context budget fastest; prune results you've used and compact before the agent drifts.
explanation: Context is a fixed budget with diminishing returns: the four big lease sections stayed in the request as raw tool results, and as the token count grew the model's recall of the original instructions degraded until it reached for the wrong tool and gave up. Nothing errored, which rules out overflow. The fix is to clear each result once it has been used and compact before the next step. Option a is the trap: a clearer description cannot explain four correct selections followed by drift.

stem: A product-help assistant returns answers in exactly the JSON your parser expects, and its wording is consistent. But on some questions it drifts into giving general legal advice that is outside the product's remit. Which technique is missing?

choices.text: A JSON schema in `output_config.format`, so the response shape is enforced on every reply
choices.reason: The shape is already right. A schema constrains structure; it says nothing about which topics the assistant should take on.

choices.text: Three to five examples of good answers, so Claude picks up the pattern more reliably
choices.reason: Examples steer "output format, tone, and structure", which are already fine here. The failure is content scope.

choices.text: A higher `effort` level, so Claude reasons more carefully before answering each question
choices.reason: Effort changes how much work goes into a response, not the boundaries of the assistant's role.

choices.text: System-prompt instructions that set the assistant's role and what is in and out of scope
choices.reason: Correct: "Setting a role in the system prompt focuses Claude's behavior and tone for your use case", and the page's first principle is to be clear and direct about what you want.

takeaway: Diagnose first: wrong shape needs a constraint, drifting content needs a scoped system prompt.
explanation: Name the failure before picking the technique. Here the shape and consistency are fine, so schemas and examples have nothing to fix; the content is drifting outside the assistant's remit, which is what a system prompt that sets the role and scope addresses. Option a is the trap: structured outputs are the reflex for "JSON assistant" problems, but they only constrain form.
